text: Never confuse stocks and mutual funds again. Same ten thousand rupees, two very different rides.
Equity means owning shares of a company. Buy one share, and you own a tiny piece of that business.
A mutual fund is a basket. Thousands of people pool their money, and a fund manager buys many stocks or bonds for all of them.
Here is the twist. An equity mutual fund also buys equity. The real difference is who picks, and how many.
Say Priya and Kiran each have ten thousand rupees. Priya buys seven shares of one company herself, through her demat account.
Kiran puts his ten thousand in a Nifty fifty index fund. He gets units, priced at the fund's N. A. V., and owns a slice of fifty companies.
Now bad news hits that one company, and its share falls thirty percent. Priya loses about three thousand rupees. For Kiran, it is one stock out of fifty, a much smaller dent.
But if that company doubles, Priya's money doubles too. Kiran gets only a small part of that gain. Higher risk, higher possible reward.
Costs. Stocks have brokerage and other charges each time you trade. Mutual funds take a yearly fee, called the expense ratio.
Tax is the same for both. Sell within a year, and pay twenty percent. After a year, twelve point five percent, on gains above one point two five lakh a year.
So who should pick what? No time to research? Start a mutual fund SIP. Love studying companies, and can handle big swings? Direct stocks. Many investors do both.
